notes.h: Why plants need transport, and the root and shoot systems
notes.b: A plant takes in materials at one end and uses them at the other, so it needs pipes to move them. Two transport tissues, xylem and phloem, do this job, and they join the plant's two main parts: the root system and the shoot system.
points: A large plant has a small surface area to volume ratio (its outer surface is small compared with the amount of living tissue inside), so diffusion alone cannot supply all its cells. There is more on this in Levels of organisation.

Roots take in water and minerals from the soil, but these are needed in the leaves. Leaves make sugar, but this is needed in the roots, growing tips, flowers, fruits and storage organs, so materials must travel both ways.
Xylem and phloem, the two transport tissues, link the roots and the leaves, so that each end gets what it cannot make or collect for itself.
The root system, everything below ground, anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals through root hairs, and often stores food, e.g. the swollen root of a carrot.
The shoot system (stem, leaves, buds and flowers) holds the leaves up to the light, carries out photosynthesis and gas exchange, transports materials between roots and leaves, and reproduces.

The two systems are joined by continuous vascular tissue (the transport tissue): the xylem and phloem of the root run up through the stem and branch out into every leaf as the veins, giving an unbroken pipeline from root hair to leaf cell.
notes.tip: Remember that xylem carries water and minerals, never sugar, while phloem carries sucrose. Keep the two jobs apart from the start.

notes.b: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job. Every plant organ is built from just three tissue types, dermal, ground and vascular, arranged in the same order from outside to inside. Exams ask you to label all three on a drawing.
points: Dermal tissue is the outer protective layer, so it is the first thing to meet the outside world. In young roots, stems and leaves it is the epidermis, usually one cell thick.

In leaves and stems the epidermis is covered by a waxy, waterproof cuticle that cuts water loss and keeps out pathogens. It contains stomata, pores that each lie between two guard cells, for gas exchange.

In roots the epidermis has no cuticle, and some epidermal cells grow out as root hairs for absorbing water and minerals. In woody stems the epidermis is replaced by bark, which is pierced by lenticels.
Ground tissue makes up the bulk of the plant between the dermal and vascular tissue. It is mostly made of living, thin-walled cells with large vacuoles (fluid-filled sacs).

The job of ground tissue depends on its position: photosynthesis in the mesophyll (the middle layer) of the leaf and in green stems; storage of starch and water in the root cortex, stem pith and potato tubers; and support, because its cells are kept firm (turgid) by water pressure.
Vascular tissue is the transport tissue: xylem carries water and dissolved minerals, and phloem carries dissolved food, mainly sucrose.
Xylem and phloem lie together in groups called vascular bundles in the stem and leaf, and in a central core in the root. Xylem also supports the plant.
notes.tip: When asked to label a root or stem section, name the tissue type (dermal, ground or vascular) as well as the structure, for example cortex (ground tissue). Questions also ask which tissue type xylem and phloem belong to: vascular.

notes.b: Xylem is the plant's water pipe. Every feature of its cells, from being hollow to having hard walls, is there so that water can rise from the roots to the leaves without obstruction and without the pipe collapsing.
points: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots, up the stem, to the leaves, in one direction only, which is upwards, because the leaves are where water is lost and used.
Xylem is made of two kinds of cell, both dead and hollow when mature, with no cytoplasm, nucleus or cell membrane, so water flows through them without obstruction.
Xylem vessels are long continuous tubes formed from a column of cells joined end to end, whose end walls have broken down. This makes one open pipe.
Tracheids are single long, narrow cells with tapering ends. Water passes from one tracheid to the next through thin areas in the walls called pits.
Pits in the side walls let water move sideways between neighbouring vessels and tracheids, and out to the surrounding cells, so water can bypass a blocked tube.
The cell walls are thickened with lignin, a hard, waterproof substance, laid down in rings, spirals or as a solid layer with pits.

Lignin stops the vessels collapsing inwards when the water in them is under tension, pulled from above. It makes xylem the main supporting tissue of woody plants: wood is xylem. There is more on this tension in Transport of water and minerals.

Diagram: a longitudinal view of a xylem vessel (a long open tube with no end walls, spiral or ring thickening of lignin and pits) beside a tracheid (tapering ends, pits); label lignin, pit, no end wall and hollow lumen (the empty space inside).
notes.tip: Xylem is dead; phloem is living. Students often swap these. Exams ask you to relate the structure of a xylem vessel to its function, so link each feature to a reason: hollow with no end walls for free flow, lignin for strength.

notes.b: Phloem is the plant's food-delivery system. Unlike xylem, its cells are alive, and it relies on a partnership between two cell types: the tube that carries the sap and the companion cell that powers it.
points: Phloem carries dissolved food, mainly sucrose and also amino acids, from the leaves, where it is made, to the parts that use or store it. It can carry food upwards or downwards, because roots and fruits lie on either side of the leaves.

Sieve tubes are columns of living sieve tube elements joined end to end. Their end walls are perforated with many small holes, forming sieve plates, through which the sap flows from one cell to the next.
A mature sieve tube element has a thin layer of cytoplasm but no nucleus and very few organelles, which leaves room for the sap to flow.
Each sieve tube element has a companion cell beside it, joined to it by many fine connections through the walls, so the two can exchange substances.

The companion cell has a nucleus, dense cytoplasm and many mitochondria. It keeps the sieve tube element alive, which has no nucleus of its own, and supplies the ATP (energy) needed to load sucrose into the sieve tube. There is more on this in Transport of CO₂ and photosynthetic products.
Phloem cell walls are cellulose only, not lignified (not strengthened with lignin), so phloem gives little support. In a woody stem the phloem lies just inside the bark.

Diagram: a longitudinal view of two sieve tube elements end to end, with a sieve plate between them and a companion cell alongside; label sieve tube element, sieve plate, cytoplasm, companion cell and nucleus (in the companion cell only).
notes.tip: Sieve tube elements have no nucleus; the companion cell has one. Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids, not glucose, and it moves food in both directions, not upwards only.

notes.b: Because the two tissues sit side by side but do opposite kinds of job, examiners like to ask for the differences. Each pair of points below sets one feature of xylem against the same feature of phloem.
points: Cells: xylem vessels and tracheids are dead and hollow, so water can flow through; sieve tube elements and companion cells are living, so they can load sucrose using energy.
Walls: xylem walls are thickened with lignin, which is why they are strong; phloem walls are cellulose only.
End walls: xylem vessels have none, so water flows freely; sieve tubes have sieve plates, perforated walls the sap passes through.
Contents: xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries sucrose and amino acids in solution.
Direction: xylem moves water upwards only, from roots to leaves; phloem moves food up or down, from where it is made or stored to where it is used.
Support: xylem supports the plant; phloem gives little support.
notes.tip: In a comparison, make each point a pair, naming both tissues, for example: xylem is dead, phloem is living. Avoid answers that describe only one tissue.

notes.b: The root has to find water in the soil and get it into the plant, so its structure is built for absorption and for holding on. Working from the tip inwards shows how each part suits its job.
points: The root anchors the plant in the soil, absorbs water and minerals, transports them to the stem, and may store food.
A root cap protects the delicate growing tip as it pushes through the soil. Just behind it is meristematic tissue whose cells divide, so the root grows in length.
Root hairs develop a little further back, on the region that has stopped growing, so they are not torn off as the root moves forward.

Each root hair is a long, thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell. There are thousands of them, giving a huge surface area for absorption, and they grow between soil particles in close contact with the film of soil water.

The root hair's wall is thin and has no cuticle, so water passes in easily. Its large vacuole holds cell sap more concentrated than the soil water, so water enters by osmosis. Its many mitochondria supply ATP for the active transport of mineral ions.

The root cortex is a wide zone of ground tissue made of large, thin-walled, loosely packed living cells with air spaces between them. Water and minerals pass across it from the root hairs to the xylem, and it stores food, often as starch.

The air spaces in the cortex let oxygen from the soil air reach the cells for respiration. The innermost single layer of the cortex, the endodermis, surrounds the vascular tissue and controls what passes into the xylem.

In the centre of the root the xylem forms a star or X shape, with the phloem in groups between its arms. This central core resists the pulling forces on a root as the shoot is blown about, as the core of a rope does.

Diagram: a transverse section (a slice across) of a young root of a broad-leaved (dicotyledonous) plant, labelled epidermis (dermal tissue), root hair, cortex (ground tissue), endodermis, xylem and phloem (vascular tissue); label the three tissue types by name as well as the structures.
notes.tip: Root hairs are extensions of single epidermal cells, not separate cells and not tiny roots; they have no cuticle and no chloroplasts. Exams ask you to relate a root hair's structure to its function: large surface area, thin wall, concentrated sap, mitochondria.

notes.b: The stem is the link between roots and leaves. It has to hold the leaves up to the light and carry materials in both directions, so it combines strength with transport tissue.
points: The stem supports the leaves and flowers, holding the leaves up to the light and the flowers up for pollination. It carries water and minerals up in the xylem and food up or down in the phloem, between the roots and the leaves.
The stem may store food, as the potato tuber does, since it is a swollen underground stem, and if it is green it photosynthesises because it contains chloroplasts.
The epidermis on the outside of a stem is dermal tissue with a waxy cuticle, which protects the stem and reduces water loss. In a woody stem it is replaced by bark.
The cortex, just inside the epidermis, and the pith in the centre are both ground tissue. Their living cells store food and water and help support the stem when they are turgid (firm with water).
The vascular bundles are arranged in a ring near the outside of the stem. In each bundle the phloem is on the outside and the xylem on the inside.
The ring of strong tissue near the edge resists bending as the stem is blown sideways, as a hollow tube does.

Diagram: a transverse section of a young, non-woody stem, labelled epidermis and cuticle (dermal tissue), cortex and pith (ground tissue), and a vascular bundle with phloem outside and xylem inside (vascular tissue).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to draw a transverse section of a root or stem and label the dermal, ground and vascular tissues. In the stem, remember the position: phloem outside, xylem inside, bundles in a ring.

notes.b: Woody stems are wrapped in bark, which is tough but also seals the living cells beneath from the air. Lenticels are the gaps that solve this problem, and they are the plant structure other than stomata through which gases are exchanged.
points: A lenticel is a small raised pore in the bark of a woody stem. Lenticels are also found on some roots, on potato tubers, and as the speckles on apple skins.
A lenticel is a patch of loosely packed cells with air spaces between them, so gases can pass through easily.

Bark is waterproof and airtight, so the living cells beneath it, including the phloem, would be cut off from air. Lenticels allow gas exchange by diffusion: oxygen in for respiration and carbon dioxide out.
A small amount of water vapour is also lost through lenticels.
Lenticels stay open all the time, because unlike stomata they have no guard cells and cannot close.
Examples: the horizontal lines on the bark of birch and cherry trees are lenticels.
notes.tip: Lenticels are not stomata: they are in bark, have no guard cells and can't close. If a question asks for a structure other than stomata where gases are exchanged, the answer is lenticels.

notes.h: The leaf: functions and external structure
notes.b: The leaf is the plant's food factory, and its shape and its connections to the stem both follow from that job. Before looking inside, it helps to see what the leaf does and how its outside suits it.
points: The leaf carries out photosynthesis, gas exchange (CO₂ in and oxygen out, in the light) and transpiration, which pulls water up the plant. There is more on this in Transport of water and minerals.
The leaf is a thin, flat, broad blade. This gives a large surface area to absorb light and CO₂, and a short distance for gases to diffuse.
The leaf stalk (petiole) holds the blade out towards the light so it catches more of it, and carries the vascular tissue into the blade.
The midrib and veins are vascular bundles that bring water and minerals in and take sucrose away, and their network supports the blade.
notes.tip: Exams ask for ways the leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. Pair each feature with its reason, for example broad flat blade, so large area for light and short diffusion distance.

notes.h: The leaf: layers from top to bottom
notes.b: A transverse section of a leaf shows layers, each with its own job. Light enters from the top, so the layers are arranged to let light through first and to put the photosynthetic cells where light is strongest.
points: The waxy cuticle on the upper, and usually the lower, epidermis is waterproof and reduces water loss by evaporation. It is transparent, so light passes through, and it is usually thicker on the upper surface, which faces the sun.
The upper epidermis is one layer of transparent cells with no chloroplasts (the green structures where photosynthesis happens), letting light through to the cells below, and it has few or no stomata.

The palisade mesophyll is one or two layers of tall, column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts. It lies just below the upper epidermis, where light is strongest, and most photosynthesis takes place here.

The spongy mesophyll is made of irregular, loosely packed cells with fewer chloroplasts and large air spaces between them. The air spaces connect to the stomata and let CO₂, oxygen and water vapour diffuse through the leaf.
The moist cell surfaces of the spongy mesophyll are where CO₂ dissolves before entering the cells and where water evaporates.
The vascular bundle, or vein, has xylem on the upper side, bringing water and minerals to the cells that need them, and phloem on the lower side, carrying sucrose away.
notes.tip: The palisade layer, not the spongy layer, does most photosynthesis; the spongy layer is for gas diffusion. A common question asks where most photosynthesis occurs and why: palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts and sit where light is strongest.

notes.h: The leaf: stomata and the lower epidermis
notes.b: A leaf needs CO₂ from the air, but any opening to the air also lets water escape. The leaf's answer is to put most of its pores on the underside and to let guard cells control them.
points: The lower epidermis contains most of the stomata. Each stoma (plural stomata) is a pore between two bean-shaped guard cells, which, unlike other epidermal cells, contain chloroplasts.
The guard cells open and close the pore. There is more on how they do this in Transport of water and minerals.
Stomata on the shaded lower surface lose less water than they would on the sunny upper surface, because it is cooler there.

Diagram: a transverse section of a leaf, labelled cuticle, upper epidermis (dermal tissue), palisade and spongy mesophyll with air spaces (ground tissue), vascular bundle with xylem above and phloem below (vascular tissue), lower epidermis, stoma and guard cells.

Diagram: a surface view of the lower epidermis showing a stoma between two guard cells (with chloroplasts) surrounded by irregular epidermal cells; label stoma, guard cell, chloroplast and epidermal cell.
notes.tip: When you draw the leaf section, label the three tissue types by name and show xylem above phloem in the vein. Remember guard cells contain chloroplasts, unlike the other epidermal cells.

keyTerms.definition: The outer protective tissue of a plant, the epidermis in young roots, stems and leaves, and bark in woody stems.
The bulk of a plant's tissue between the dermal and vascular tissue, made of living thin-walled cells that photosynthesise, store food and water, or support the plant.
The transport tissue of a plant, made of xylem and phloem, grouped into vascular bundles or, in the root, a central core.
A waxy, waterproof layer on the outside of the epidermis that reduces water loss and keeps out pathogens.
A pore in the epidermis, bounded by two guard cells, through which gases diffuse in and out of the leaf.
One of two bean-shaped cells that surround a stoma and open or close it by changing their turgor.
A small raised pore in the bark of a woody stem, with loosely packed cells, that allows gas exchange because bark is airtight.
A long, thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell of a root that absorbs water and minerals over a large surface area.
The wide zone of ground tissue in a root, between the root hairs and the endodermis, that transports water and minerals, stores food and has air spaces.
The innermost single layer of the root cortex, which surrounds the vascular tissue and controls what passes into the xylem.
Vascular tissue made of dead, hollow vessels and tracheids, lignified, that carries water and dissolved minerals upwards.
A long continuous tube of dead, hollow cells, formed from a column of cells whose end walls have broken down, with lignified walls.
A single long, narrow, dead xylem cell with tapering ends and pits, through which water passes to the next tracheid.
A hard, waterproof substance that thickens the walls of xylem and stops the vessels collapsing.
A thin area in the wall of a xylem vessel or tracheid through which water passes sideways to neighbouring cells.
Vascular tissue of living sieve tube elements and companion cells that carries sucrose and amino acids up or down the plant.
A living phloem cell with no nucleus, joined end to end to others to form a sieve tube.
A perforated end wall between sieve tube elements through which phloem sap flows.
A living cell beside a sieve tube element, with a nucleus and many mitochondria, that keeps it alive and loads sucrose into it.
Tall, column-shaped leaf cells packed with chloroplasts, just below the upper epidermis, where most photosynthesis takes place.
Loosely packed leaf cells with large air spaces that connect to the stomata and allow gases to diffuse through the leaf.

questions.prompt: Give two structural differences between xylem vessels and sieve tubes, and state what each tissue transports.
questions.model: Xylem vessels are dead and hollow, with walls thickened by lignin, and they have no end walls because the end walls have broken down. Sieve tubes are made of living cells, with cellulose-only walls that are not lignified, and their end walls are perforated by sieve plates. Xylem vessels transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from the roots to the leaves. Sieve tubes transport sucrose and amino acids in solution, from the leaves to the parts of the plant that use or store them.

questions.prompt: Draw a labelled diagram of a transverse section through a leaf. Label one example each of dermal, ground and vascular tissue, and explain how two of the structures you have labelled are adapted to their functions.
questions.model: The diagram shows a transverse section of a leaf, labelled as follows: the upper epidermis and cuticle (dermal tissue); the palisade mesophyll and spongy mesophyll (ground tissue); and a vascular bundle with xylem above and phloem below (vascular tissue). It also shows the lower epidermis with a stoma between two guard cells. The palisade mesophyll is adapted for photosynthesis: its cells are tall and column-shaped and packed with chloroplasts, and they lie just below the upper epidermis, where light is strongest, so most photosynthesis takes place there. The spongy mesophyll is adapted for gas exchange: its cells are loosely packed, with large air spaces that connect to the stomata, so CO₂, oxygen and water vapour can diffuse through the leaf, and its moist cell surfaces let CO₂ dissolve before it enters the cells.

questions.prompt: Explain how a root hair is adapted for absorbing water and minerals, and state the function of the root cortex.
questions.model: A root hair is a long, thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell, and there are thousands of them, so the surface area for absorption is very large. Its wall is thin and has no cuticle, so water passes in easily. Its large vacuole contains cell sap more concentrated than the soil water, so water enters by osmosis. Its many mitochondria supply the ATP needed for the active transport of mineral ions. The root cortex carries water and minerals across from the root hairs to the xylem, stores food, often as starch, and has air spaces that let oxygen from the soil air reach its cells for respiration.
